lessons.title: Calculating the True Landed Cost
lessons.body: When you buy a small Chinese machine, the price you see on Alibaba or from a local dealer is never the final amount you pay. The true landed cost includes the machine price, shipping, import duties, clearing fees, transport to your workshop, and any minor repairs or missing parts. For example, a block-making machine advertised at $1,200 FOB (Free On Board) from China will cost you more. Sea freight to Mombasa or Lagos might be $300, import duty at 25% of the CIF value (cost, insurance, freight) adds another $375, clearing agent fees $150, and local transport $100. Your true landed cost is now $2,125 â nearly double the sticker price. Always ask for a CIF quote and then calculate duties yourself using your country's tariff code. In Kenya, for instance, many small machines fall under HS code 8474 with a 25% duty and 16% VAT. In Nigeria, duty can be 10-20% plus 7.5% VAT. Use a simple spreadsheet: list machine cost, freight, insurance, duty, VAT, clearing, transport, and a 10% contingency for surprises. If you are buying locally from a dealer, the landed cost is already baked into their price, but you should still ask what warranty and spare parts are included. Never forget the cost of power: a 3-phase machine may need a transformer or generator, adding $500-$1,500. Also budget for installation and training. A true landed cost calculation prevents you from sinking all your money into the machine and having nothing left to operate. Write down every number. If you cannot afford the true landed cost, you cannot afford the machine.

lessons.title: Micro-Leasing and Asset Financing Options
lessons.body: Micro-leasing is when a company buys the machine and rents it to you for a weekly or monthly fee, with the option to own it at the end. In many African countries, specialized asset finance companies like Rentworks in South Africa, or microfinance banks in Kenya and Nigeria, offer this. For example, a small maize mill costing $2,000 might be leased for $80 per week over 12 months. At the end, you pay a balloon payment of $200 and own it. The total cost is $4,160 â double the cash price â but you did not need collateral or a large lump sum. Asset financing works similarly but is often structured as a hire purchase. You pay a 20-30% deposit, then fixed monthly installments over 12-24 months. The machine itself is the collateral. In Ghana, companies like Sinapi Aba Trust offer asset financing for agro-processing machines. In Tanzania, CRDB Bank has a 'Imbeju' product for small businesses. The key is to read the contract: check the interest rate (often 2-4% per month), the total cost of credit, and what happens if you miss a payment. Some leases require you to insure the machine. Others charge a penalty of 5% per late installment. Before signing, calculate your monthly profit from the machine. If the machine earns you $300 per month and the lease is $150, you have $150 left for raw materials and your own income. If the lease is $250, you are too close to the edge. Always negotiate a grace period of one month before the first payment. Ask if you can pay weekly instead of monthly to match your cash flow. Micro-leasing is a powerful tool if you treat it as a business partnership, not a rescue loan.

lessons.title: Bank Loans and Collateral Requirements
lessons.body: Banks in Africa rarely lend to small businesses without collateral. For a machine loan, the bank will ask for land, a building, a vehicle, or a fixed deposit. If you do not have these, you have three options. First, use a group loan: join a cooperative or savings group where members guarantee each other. In Ethiopia, the 'Equb' system works this way. Second, use a credit guarantee scheme. In Kenya, the Credit Guarantee Scheme for SMEs covers up to 50% of the loan. In Nigeria, the Development Bank of Nigeria provides wholesale funds to banks for on-lending to SMEs. Third, build a credit history with a small loan first. Take a $500 loan, repay it in three months, then ask for $2,000. When you apply, the bank will want a business plan, cash flow projections, and invoices for the machine. They may also require the machine to be insured and registered in the bank's name until you finish paying. Interest rates vary: 12-18% per year in Kenya, 20-30% in Nigeria, 10-15% in South Africa. A $2,000 loan at 18% over 18 months means a monthly payment of about $128. You will pay $304 in interest. That is acceptable if the machine generates at least $400 per month. But if the bank asks for a 20% deposit and you do not have it, do not borrow from a loan shark to pay it. Instead, save for six months. Also, avoid 'loan insurance' that adds 5% to the loan. Ask for a amortization schedule. If the bank officer cannot explain it, walk away. A bank loan is cheaper than micro-leasing but harder to get. Start building your relationship with a bank today, even if you only open a savings account and deposit $20 weekly.

lessons.title: Vendor Credit and Dealer Financing
lessons.body: Some Chinese machine vendors and local dealers offer credit directly. This is called vendor credit or supplier financing. For example, a dealer in Nairobi might sell you a $1,500 welding machine and allow you to pay 50% now and the rest over six months with 10% interest. The dealer keeps the machine's serial number registered until you finish paying. This is simpler than a bank loan because the dealer knows the machine and trusts you more than a bank does. To get vendor credit, you need a relationship. Buy small spare parts from the dealer first. Pay cash on time. Then ask for terms. In China, many factories on Alibaba offer 'Trade Assurance' with 30% deposit and 70% before shipping. That is not credit. But some will accept 30% deposit and the balance in 60 days if you have a history. For local dealers, ask for a 'hire purchase agreement'. It should state the total price, deposit, installments, interest, and what happens if you default. In Uganda, companies like Toyota Uganda (for generators) offer leasing through their finance arm. In Senegal, dealers for rice milling machines often give 3-month credit to cooperatives. Always get the agreement in writing. Never rely on a handshake. If the dealer asks for a post-dated cheque or a promissory note, understand that they can sue you if you default. But vendor credit can be the fastest way to get a machine. Use it for machines that will pay for themselves quickly â like a popcorn machine that earns daily cash. Avoid vendor credit for machines that take months to generate income, like a brick-making machine that needs curing time. And always ask: what is the penalty for late payment? If it is more than 2% per month, negotiate.

lessons.title: Partnerships and Cooperative Ownership
lessons.body: If you cannot afford a machine alone, partner with others. A cooperative of five tailors can buy one industrial sewing machine for $800, each contributing $160. They share the machine on a schedule: Monday and Tuesday for one, Wednesday for another, and so on. The machine earns more because it is used every day. In Rwanda, the 'Umuganda' spirit of collective work has led to many such cooperatives. In Kenya, chamas (savings groups) often buy assets together. The key is a written agreement. It must state: who contributed how much, how the machine will be used, who maintains it, what happens if someone wants to leave, and how profits are shared. For example, a group of five maize millers buys a $3,000 mill. Each pays $600. They agree that each person mills for two days per week and pays $10 per day into a maintenance fund. After one year, they sell the mill and split the proceeds according to contribution. Or they keep it and continue. Another model is a partnership where one person provides the machine and another provides the workspace and labour. They split profits 50-50. This works for a car wash with a Chinese pressure washer. But partnerships fail when there is no clear leader. Choose a chairperson and a treasurer. Keep a bank account for the machine. Record every payment. If you buy as a cooperative, you may also qualify for government grants or NGO support. In Tanzania, the Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO) gives matching grants to cooperatives. In Ethiopia, the Federal Micro and Small Enterprise Development Agency supports groups. Always register your group formally if you want to access these funds. Do not let friendship replace paperwork. A simple one-page contract signed by all members is enough to prevent most disputes.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping: Starting with One Machine
lessons.body: Bootstrapping means starting with what you have, not what you wish you had. If you only have $200, do not look at $2,000 machines. Look at a $150 manual block-making machine or a $100 popcorn maker. Your first machine should be small enough that you can pay cash and still have money for raw materials. For example, a hand-operated maize sheller costs $80 in Kampala. You can shell 200 kg of maize per day and charge $0.50 per kg. That is $100 per day gross. After paying for transport and your own labour, you save $50 per day. In 40 days, you have $2,000. Now you can buy a motorized sheller. This is the bootstrap cycle: buy small, earn, save, upgrade. Do not take a loan for your first machine. Use your own savings or a small family loan. The goal is to prove the business works before you take on debt. Start by renting the machine out to others. If you buy a welding machine, do not just weld your own gates. Weld for neighbours at $5 per joint. Reinvest every dollar into consumables and spare parts. Keep a notebook of daily income and expenses. After three months, calculate your return on investment. If you spent $200 and earned $600, your ROI is 200%. Now you can approach a bank or lease company with proof. Bootstrapping also means buying used. A used Chinese machine from a local dealer might cost half the price of new. Check the motor, bearings, and belts. If it runs for an hour without overheating, it is likely fine. Buy one machine, not two. Master it. Then expand. Many successful African workshops started with a single sewing machine or a single grinding mill. Your first machine is your teacher. It will show you what breaks, what sells, and what customers want. Only after that should you think about financing a bigger one.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Financing Your Machine Purchase

This practical reference consolidates the key numbers, documents, and decision rules you need when financing a small Chinese machine â whether a maize mill, rice thresher, oil press, block-making machine, or sewing unit. It is designed as a working document: print it, take it to the bank, the dealer, and the cooperative meeting. The goal is simple â know your true cost, know your options, and never sign without checking the numbers yourself.

1. The True Landed Cost Formula

Many African buyers compare only the FOB (Free On Board) price quoted by the Chinese supplier. That is a mistake. The true landed cost includes freight, insurance, customs duty, clearing, inland transport, installation, and the cost of financing itself. In Kenya, for example, a machine with a CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) value of KES 200,000 will attract import duty (often 0â25% depending on HS code), VAT at 16%, IDF at 3.5% of CIF, RDL at 2% of CIF, and clearing agent fees. The final landed cost can be 40â70% above the FOB price.

Formula: Landed Cost = FOB + Freight + Insurance + Duty + VAT + IDF + RDL + Clearing + Inland Transport + Installation + Financing Cost.

The lesson is clear: if you budget only the FOB price, you will run out of money before the machine is installed. Always add 40â70% for a realistic landed cost in most African markets.

2. Financing Option Comparison

There are six main routes to financing a small machine in Africa. Each has different collateral requirements, speed, and total cost. The table below compares them using real market conditions from Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana.

Financing Option Typical Cost Collateral / Security Speed Best For
Micro-Leasing (asset finance) 18â35% APR effective Machine itself (leased asset) 1â3 weeks Startups with no land title
Bank Loan (SME) 14â24% APR Land title, fixed deposit, or guarantor 4â12 weeks Registered businesses with collateral
Vendor / Dealer Credit 0â15% effective Down payment 30â50% 1â7 days Buyers with strong dealer relationship
Cooperative / SACCO 10â18% APR Group guarantee, savings history 2â6 weeks Members of active cooperatives
Bootstrapping (one machine) 0% interest None Immediate First-time buyers with savings
Partnership / Joint Ownership 0â10% (opportunity cost) Written agreement 1â4 weeks Groups of 2â5 entrepreneurs

Sources: Central Bank of Kenya Bank Supervision Reports (2023â2024); Bank of Ghana Monetary Policy Reports; Nigeria's Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) MSME finance data; author's interviews with equipment dealers in Nairobi and Lagos, 2024.

3. Bank Loans and Collateral Reality

In most African markets, banks will not lend against the machine itself unless it is a registered asset with a serial number and a formal lease agreement. They want land, a fixed deposit, or a salary guarantor. The table below shows what banks actually accept as collateral in three major markets.

Country Most Accepted Collateral Typical Loan Size (USD) Interest Rate (APR) Key Requirement
Kenya Land title (freehold/leasehold), fixed deposit, chattel mortgage 1,000 â 50,000 14â24% 6+ months bank statements, CRB clearance
Nigeria Landed property, fixed deposit, third-party guarantor 500 â 30,000 18â30% BVN, TIN, business registration (CAC)
Ghana Land title, vehicle, fixed deposit, group guarantee 500 â 25,000 20â32% Ghana Card, business operating permit

Sources: Central Bank of Kenya, "Bank Supervision Annual Report 2023"; Central Bank of Nigeria, "Guide to Charges by Banks and Other Financial Institutions" (2020, updated 2024); Bank of Ghana, "Credit Reporting and Collateral Registry Guidelines," 2023.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Never Sign a Blank Loan or Lease Form

Some micro-leasing companies and dealers in East and West Africa ask borrowers to sign blank or partially completed loan forms "for processing." This is illegal in most jurisdictions and has been used to inflate interest rates, add hidden fees, or seize machines without notice. Always demand a fully completed contract with the total cost of credit, the APR, the repayment schedule, and the repossession terms written in plain language. Keep a signed copy. If a lender refuses, walk away. Report to the Central Bank or the national consumer protection agency.

4. Vendor Credit and Dealer Financing

Many Chinese machine dealers in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, and Dar es Salaam now offer in-house credit. The typical structure is 30â50% down payment, with the balance paid over 3â12 months. The effective interest rate is often hidden in the markup. For example, a machine quoted at USD 2,000 cash may be sold on credit at USD 2,400 over 6 months â an effective APR of roughly 40%. Always ask for the cash price and the credit price side by side, then calculate the difference as a percentage of the cash price.

5. Partnerships and Cooperative Ownership

For machines costing more than USD 3,000, a partnership of 3â5 people can spread the risk and the cost. The critical document is a written partnership agreement that covers: who contributes how much, who operates the machine, how revenue is split, how maintenance is funded, what happens if one partner wants out, and how the machine is valued if sold. Without this, partnerships collapse. Cooperatives and SACCOs are often the best route because they already have group guarantee structures and savings history that banks recognize.

6. Bootstrapping: Starting with One Machine

The safest financing is no financing. If you can save and buy one small machine â a maize mill at USD 800, a sewing machine at USD 300, a block maker at USD 1,200 â you avoid interest, collateral, and debt risk. Use the machine to generate cash flow, then reinvest in a second machine. This is the slowest route but the most resilient. Many successful African agribusinesses started with one machine and grew through retained earnings. The key is to keep the machine running at high utilization â at least 60% of available hours â so it pays for itself within 12â18 months.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Calculate true landed cost â FOB + freight + insurance + duty + VAT + clearing + transport + installation + financing. Add 40â70% to FOB.
  2. Compare all six financing routes â leasing, bank loan, vendor credit, cooperative, partnership, bootstrapping. Get at least two written quotes.
  3. Demand the APR in writing â not just the monthly payment. Calculate total cost of credit yourself.
  4. Check collateral requirements early â land title, fixed deposit, or guarantor. Do not waste time on banks that will reject you.
  5. Never sign blank forms â insist on a complete contract with repossession and default terms.
  6. For partnerships, write the agreement first â contributions, roles, revenue split, exit terms, and machine valuation method.
  7. Test machine utilization â can you keep it running 60%+ of available hours? If not, the financing will fail.
  8. Keep a cash reserve â at least 3 months of repayments plus maintenance costs before you sign.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Central Bank of Kenya â Bank Supervision Reports and SME Finance Data
  • Central Bank of Nigeria â Guide to Charges and MSME Finance Guidelines
  • Bank of Ghana â Credit Reporting and Collateral Registry Guidelines
  • African Development Bank â SME and Agribusiness Finance Reports
  • FAO â Agricultural Machinery and Equipment Financing in Africa (PDF)

This practical reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course "Small Chinese Machines," module "Financing Your Machine Purchase." Always verify current duty rates, interest rates, and regulations with the relevant national authority before committing funds.

quiz.q: What is the true landed cost of a machine?
options: A) The price on the vendor's website
B) The machine price plus shipping, duties, clearing, and transport
quiz.explanation: Landed cost includes all costs to get the machine to your workshop, not just the sticker price.

quiz.q: If a machine costs $1,200 FOB, sea freight is $300, import duty is 25% of CIF, and clearing is $150, what is the CIF value?
quiz.explanation: CIF = FOB + freight + insurance (assume insurance is zero here) = $1,200 + $300 = $1,500.

quiz.q: Why should you add a 10% contingency to your landed cost calculation?
options: A) To pay for unexpected repairs or missing parts
C) To cover the vendor's profit
D) To pay for your own salary
quiz.explanation: Contingency covers surprises like damaged parts, extra clearing fees, or minor repairs.

quiz.q: What is micro-leasing?
options: A) A short-term loan from a bank
B) Renting a machine with an option to own it
C) Buying a machine with cash
quiz.explanation: Micro-leasing involves weekly or monthly payments with ownership at the end.

quiz.q: In a micro-lease, what is a balloon payment?
options: B) A large final payment to own the machine
C) A penalty for late payment
quiz.explanation: A balloon payment is a lump sum at the end of the lease to transfer ownership.

quiz.q: What is the typical interest rate range for micro-leasing in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Micro-leasing often charges 2-4% per month, which is higher than bank loans.

quiz.q: What is asset financing?
options: A) A loan to buy raw materials
B) A hire purchase agreement where the machine is collateral
quiz.explanation: Asset financing uses the machine itself as security for the loan.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate the total cost of credit before signing a lease?
options: A) To compare with cash price and ensure profitability
quiz.explanation: Total cost of credit shows the real amount you pay, which affects your profit.

quiz.q: What is a common collateral requirement for a bank loan in Africa?
options: A) A written business plan only
B) Land, a building, or a vehicle
quiz.explanation: Banks typically require physical assets as collateral for small business loans.

quiz.q: What is a credit guarantee scheme?
options: A) A scheme where the government guarantees part of your loan
B) A scheme where you guarantee someone else's loan
C) A scheme to avoid paying interest
D) A scheme to get free machines
quiz.explanation: Credit guarantee schemes reduce bank risk by covering a portion of the loan.

quiz.q: If you borrow $2,000 at 18% annual interest over 18 months, what is the approximate monthly payment?
quiz.explanation: Using simple amortization, monthly payment is about $128.

quiz.q: What should you do if a bank asks for a 20% deposit you cannot afford?
options: A) Borrow from a loan shark
B) Save for six months and then apply
D) Skip the loan and give up
quiz.explanation: Saving for the deposit is safer than high-interest borrowing.

quiz.q: What is vendor credit?
options: A) A loan from a bank
B) Credit given by the machine dealer or supplier
quiz.explanation: Vendor credit is when the seller allows you to pay over time.

quiz.q: What is a common deposit percentage for vendor credit?
quiz.explanation: Vendors often require a significant deposit, like 30-50%, to reduce their risk.

quiz.q: Why is vendor credit often easier to get than a bank loan?
options: A) Because the vendor knows you and the machine
B) Because there is no interest
C) Because the government pays for it
D) Because you don't need to pay back
quiz.explanation: Vendors rely on relationship and knowledge of the machine, not formal collateral.

quiz.q: What should a hire purchase agreement always include?
options: B) Deposit, installments, interest, and default terms
quiz.explanation: A written agreement must detail all financial terms and consequences.

quiz.q: What is a risk of vendor credit?
options: A) The machine may be stolen
B) The vendor can sue you if you default
D) You own the machine immediately
quiz.explanation: Defaulting on vendor credit can lead to legal action or asset seizure.

quiz.q: What is a cooperative ownership model?
options: A) One person owns the machine and rents it out
B) A group of people jointly buy and share a machine
C) The government owns the machine
D) A bank owns the machine
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives pool resources to buy and share equipment.

quiz.q: What is essential in a cooperative machine ownership agreement?
options: B) A written contract stating contributions, usage, and exit terms
quiz.explanation: Written contracts prevent disputes over usage and profits.

quiz.q: How can a cooperative access government grants?
options: B) By registering formally and applying
C) By keeping the group informal
quiz.explanation: Formal registration is often required for grants and support.

quiz.q: What is bootstrapping?
options: A) Starting with a large loan
B) Starting small with your own savings and reinvesting profits
C) Buying the most expensive machine
quiz.explanation: Bootstrapping means growing your business from your own cash flow.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid a loan for your first machine?
options: A) Because loans are always bad
B) To prove the business works before taking on debt
quiz.explanation: Proving the business model reduces risk before borrowing.

quiz.q: What is a good first step if you only have $200?
options: A) Buy a $2,000 machine on credit
B) Buy a small manual machine and earn daily
D) Borrow from a loan shark
quiz.explanation: Starting small allows you to generate cash and learn the business.

quiz.q: What does ROI stand for?
quiz.explanation: ROI measures the profitability of an investment.

quiz.q: Why is keeping a daily notebook important when bootstrapping?
options: A) To show off to friends
B) To track income and expenses for decision-making
quiz.explanation: Records help you understand your cash flow and profitability.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying a used Chinese machine?
options: A) It is always better than new
B) It can cost half the price of new
C) It has a longer warranty
quiz.explanation: Used machines are cheaper, but you must inspect them carefully.

quiz.q: What should you check when buying a used machine?
quiz.explanation: These parts are critical for machine function and costly to replace.

quiz.q: What is the bootstrap cycle?
options: A) Buy big, earn, save, buy bigger
B) Buy small, earn, save, upgrade
quiz.explanation: The cycle starts small and uses profits to upgrade.

quiz.q: Why is it important to master one machine before buying another?
options: A) To avoid mistakes and understand the business
quiz.explanation: Mastering one machine teaches you maintenance, market, and profitability.

quiz.q: What is a potential downside of micro-leasing?
options: A) You own the machine immediately
B) The total cost can be double the cash price
D) You don't need to pay anything
quiz.explanation: Micro-leasing often results in a total cost much higher than buying cash.
